analysis.one_liner: Permanently bans offshore oil and gas drilling off California, Oregon, and Washington.
analysis.headline: The bill never got a committee hearing or a vote; it died in the Senate Energy Committee at the end of the 115th Congress.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill amended federal law to bar the Interior Department from ever selling a lease for oil or gas drilling in federal waters off the coasts of California, Oregon, and Washington. The aim was to permanently shield those coastlines from offshore drilling and the risk of spills. It was introduced by six Senate Democrats and referred to the Senate Energy and Natural Resources Committee, which took no further action before that Congress ended.
analysis.who_benefits: Coastal communities, fishing businesses, and tourism economies in California, Oregon, and Washington, which would be spared the spill risk and industrial activity that come with offshore drilling. The general public along the West Coast also benefits from permanently protected waters.
analysis.who_benefits_short: West Coast coastal communities and fisheries

how_it_helps.text: The bill permanently prohibits the Interior Secretary from issuing any lease for exploration, development, or production of oil or natural gas on the outer Continental Shelf off California, Oregon, or Washington.
It writes the ban directly into the Outer Continental Shelf Lands Act, so it would apply regardless of which administration set future drilling plans.

analysis.who_pays: The oil and gas industry, which would lose any possibility of leasing and drilling in federal waters off the three West Coast states, along with the federal government's foregone lease revenue and royalties from any oil or gas found there.
analysis.who_pays_short: Oil and gas companies seeking new leases

drawbacks.text: The ban permanently closes off any future domestic oil and gas development in West Coast federal waters, forgoing potential production and federal royalty revenue from those areas.

A permanent statutory ban removes the flexibility of the existing leasing process, under which each administration decides through regular five-year planning whether and where to allow drilling, weighing energy supply against environmental risk.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The benefit is a permanent, statutory shield for three state coastlines against offshore drilling and spill risk, which matters most to the fishing, tourism, and coastal communities that would bear those costs. The cost is closing a region to energy development and the revenue that could come with it. Whether that trade is worth it depends largely on how much oil and gas lies off the West Coast; the bill's supporters judged the environmental risk to coasts worth more than the potential production.

outcome.mechanism: It was introduced and referred to the Senate Energy and Natural Resources Committee, which never acted on it, so it died when the 115th Congress ended in January 2019.

narrative.text: The bill was introduced on January 4, 2017, by Sen. Dianne Feinstein with five Democratic cosponsors, and was read twice and referred to the Committee on Energy and Natural Resources.

No further action was ever taken: the bill received no subcommittee or full committee action, no floor vote, and no companion House action in the record, and it expired at the end of the 115th Congress.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: The oil and gas industry is better off because the bill died: West Coast federal waters were never placed permanently off limits, leaving that potential leasing area available to future administrations. Nothing was lost by coastal communities in the short term, since no West Coast leases were being issued at the time.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Oil and gas interests, which keep the option of West Coast drilling

for.name: Sen. Dianne Feinstein
for.role: U.S. Senator from California; bill sponsor
for.what_they_did: Sponsored the bill to permanently ban West Coast offshore oil and gas leasing.

for.name: Sens. Wyden, Cantwell, Merkley, Murray, and Harris

against.name: Senate Energy and Natural Resources Committee
against.what_they_did: Referred the bill on the day of introduction and never scheduled any hearing, markup, or vote on it.

sides.party_line_note: All six sponsors and cosponsors were Democrats, and the Republican-led Energy Committee took no action on the bill.

industries.industry: Oil and gas exploration and production companies
industries.note: The bill permanently bars them from leasing or drilling in federal waters off California, Oregon, and Washington, closing a potential new frontier. Its gain from the bill dying was continued access to that possibility, while its drilling activity would impose spill and industrialization risk on coastal communities.

industries.industry: West Coast fishing and tourism businesses
industries.note: A permanent leasing ban protects the clean coastal waters and shorelines their businesses depend on from drilling activity and the risk of oil spills.
